report:
# Dark Chocolate and Stroke Risk: What the Evidence Shows

The claim has some support from observational studies, but the evidence is mixed and not conclusive for causation.

**Supporting evidence:** A widely cited meta-analysis of five prospective cohort studies (Larsson et al., published in *Neurology*) found that high chocolate consumers had a relative risk of stroke around 0.81 (about 19% lower) compared to low consumers ([neurology.org](https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0b013e31826aacfa)). A more recent 2025 review reiterates similar pooled estimates—RR 0.81 for high vs. low intake, and 0.86 per additional 50g/week ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1696220/full)). These associations are plausible mechanistically, since cocoa flavanols improve endothelial function and lower blood pressure.

**Contradicting evidence:** However, most cohort studies rely on self-reported food-frequency questionnaires that don't distinguish dark from milk chocolate, and confounding (chocolate eaters may have healthier lifestyles or higher socioeconomic status) is a major concern. The Women's Health Study, a large prospective cohort, found **no significant association** between chocolate intake and stroke or CHD risk, and even noted a positive trend (increased risk) in older women at the highest consumption quintile ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002916522029069)). A 2023 Mendelian randomization study using genetic variants (which reduces confounding bias) found no causal relationship between dark chocolate intake and cardiovascular disease risk ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-50351-6)).

**Conclusion:** The observational link between chocolate and lower stroke risk is real in some cohorts but inconsistent, likely confounded, and not supported by causal genetic analyses. Dark chocolate may offer modest cardiovascular benefits via flavanols in moderation, but current evidence does not robustly establish that eating dark chocolate causally lowers stroke risk. Treat the claim as plausible but unproven, not established fact.
